Dracula History for Sleep 🌙 Was He Real? A Night in Transylvania

Premieres Wed 28 Oct at 5 PM ET (21:00 UTC) · About 2 hours 7 min · narrated slowly for sleep

Find it on our YouTube channel

The video goes public on the channel at the premiere time.

Was Dracula real? History for sleep: a calm, two-hour true story of Dracula, from a Transylvanian village's garlic vigil to Vlad III, the dragon's son, and Bram Stoker's notebook.

🌙 No mid-video ads, nothing to wake you.

In 1820, a London book about Wallachia added a footnote: "Dracula in the Wallachian language means Devil." Seventy years later, on a summer holiday in Whitby, a tired theatre manager named Bram Stoker copied that line into his notebook.

Tonight we spend one long, quiet night, the Eve of Saint Andrew, in an imagined village at the foot of the Carpathians, as families rub garlic on their doorframes and keep watch over it until cockcrow. Along the way we follow how a real prince's name and an old village fear met in one book: the word vampir travelling north, the official reports from Kisiljevo and Medveđa, the empress's doctor in Vienna, a rainy summer by Lake Geneva, Emily Gerard's notebooks in Transylvania, Vlad III of Wallachia, and a little library on the Yorkshire coast.

This is a quiet bedtime documentary, narrated slowly to help you relax and drift off to sleep. No loud sounds, no sudden changes and no horror: just a soft voice, slow images, and a stove glowing through a long autumn night.

About this sleep story

About 2 hours 7 min, narrated slowly for sleep, with no ad breaks. Made as history to fall asleep to: it's fine to drift off partway, and the chapters below let you find your place again.

This episode began with one small detail: a footnote in an old book about Wallachia, read in the little subscription library at Whitby in the summer of 1890, from which Bram Stoker copied the name "Dracula". We went back from that page to the village stories that came long before it, so the history could stay close to ordinary people. The customs, reports, people and quotations are real; the village and its family are imagined. Where the evidence is only likely, such as whether Stoker first met the name in Whitby or in London, the narration says so.

Sources

Researched and written for this channel from these sources. Where historians disagree, the narration says so.

  • Emily Gerard, "Transylvanian Superstitions" (The Nineteenth Century, July 1885)
  • Emily Gerard, The Land Beyond the Forest (William Blackwood and Sons, 1888)
  • William Wilkinson, An Account of the Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia (1820)
  • Johann Flückinger and others, Visum et Repertum (military report, Belgrade, 26 January 1732)
  • Augustin Calmet, Dissertations sur les apparitions… et sur les revenants et vampires (1746)
  • Gerard van Swieten, Remarques sur le vampyrisme (1755)
  • John Polidori, The Vampyre (New Monthly Magazine, 1819)
  • Bram Stoker's Notes for Dracula: A Facsimile Edition, annotated by Robert Eighteen-Bisang and Elizabeth Miller (McFarland, 2008)
  • Bram Stoker, Dracula (Archibald Constable and Co., 1897)
